html:
Directory of Works of Mercy

Introduction

We know through Sacred Scripture that “God is love” (1 Jn 4: 16). He loves himself as highest good. But we also know that his good tends to communicate itself, it is for that that God, infinite goodness, created the universe. By this work of his love, God not only participate being to the creature, but makes her fertile, giving her the power to diffuse that good by virtue of his same Love, the Holy Spirit: “the Spirit of God swept over the waters” (Gen 1:2). In this way, the universe will be able to reach the end for which it was created.

Within the goods participated by God to the creature is Freedom. It is given to spiritual beings, who by contrast to material beings, must reach their end freely. Moreover, with freedom appears the possibility of not reaching that end, or of the existential breakdown.

This possibility is made actual through sin, which is no other than the rejection of God and of his love. First a certain number of angels fell in sin, “because the devil has sinned from the beginning” (1 Jn 3: 8), afterwards, our first parents also fell, and through them, all the human race: “just as through one person sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and thus death came to all, inasmuch as all sinned” (Rom 5:12).

Before the lack of love of man, God answers with love, well then, he logically applied his justice in order to reestablish the alternated order: “The LORD God therefore banished him from the garden of Eden” (Gen 3: 23), also he was merciful when he promised a redeemer to the offspring of Eve. “In God, the Spirit of love changes the dimension of the human sin in a new gift of salvific love”. Therefore then, before the misery of the creature, the answer of God is mercy, who “in the preaching of the prophets signifies a special potency of love which is prevalent over sin and the infidelity of the chosen people.

It is interesting to recover this iidea of the divine mercy as potency of the love which conquers evil throughout the length of the history of mankind.

Our Father, who is a God “rich in Mercy” (Eph 2: 4), had mercy on the people of the covenant. From the deeds most worthy of praise of the Old Testament, we can record: the beginning of the history of the Jews, where the Israelites fall into idolatry, and in consequence are burdened by their enemies, therefore they called on Yahweh, and obtained his mercy; the prayer of Salomon at the inauguration of the temple; a part of the propheti intervention of Micah: “[he] does not persist in anger forever, but delights rather in clemency, and will again have compassion on us, treading underfoot our guilt” (Mic 7: 18-19); the securities offered by Isaiah; The supplication of the exiled; the renovation of the covenant after the exile. Physical evil as much as moral evil make the children of Israel have recourse to mercy. That is what David does for the gravity of his sin, Job in his disgrace, Esther before the threat for her people, etc….

When the fullness of time had come, by the work of the Holy Spirit, the Word was made flesh. “Christ is the revelation and the incarnation of the mercy of the Father, he then comes to reveal and to incarnate his merciful love. He reveals and incarnates therefore the mercy of God which is the potency of the love which conquers evil, by means of the greatest work of mercy ever know which is the redemption of humankind by the blood of his cross, with which he kills the root of all evil, which is sin. Work which eliminates even the effects of sin. When St. John sent two of his disciples to ask Jesus: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?” (Lk 7:19), our Lord answers: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind regain their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have the good news proclaimed to them” (Lk 7:22).

In this way, “Christ manifested man to man in the revelation of the mystery of the Father”. Our redeemer then reveals the mercy of God in accepting the cross, with which the love of the Father is concretely shown. As the old Adam rejected the love of God, so Christ is the new Adam who teaches man that only in accepting the mercy of God can he love the Father.

Our religious family, another prolongation of the Incarnation of the Word, “to incarnated in all of man”, humbly desires by means of the works of mercy to:

Continue to reveal to men the merciful love of God for mankind, and continue to incarnate it through all types of works of benevolence and with it, to alleviate many evils which befalls upon the actual man. So that moreover by the testimony ofcharity many brothers may know God “so that they may see your good deeds and glorify your heavenly Father” (Mt. 5:16).

To love God, well then the concrete love of brothers is the unique way possible to love God, as the apostle moreover affirms: “he that says he loves God, and does not love his brothers is a liar”.

Our institute by this, desires to follow the wheel of the Incarnate Word, who not only came to redeem us from sin, but subjected himself to its effects, given that he passed through this world, healing men from their physical and spiritual miseries, through which he gave a concrete proof of his mercy and of his love for thee Father.

“Mary is the one who in a singular and exceptional way experienced…mercy…and has made it possible with the sacrifice of her heart the proper participation of the revelation of Divine Mercy.

“This maternity of Mary is the economy of the grace always strong since the assent… in the Annunciation which remained without change at the foot of the Cross until the perpetual consummation of the elects.

Therefore the religious, who must have the charge of a work of mercy, whether corporal or spiritual, must imitate the Blessed Virgin Mary in her Merciful maternity.

The specific and singular end of the institute of the Incarnate Word is the evangelization of culture, and it is precisely the spiritual works of mercy that are more in symphony with this end, and are the ones that diffuse better the good.

But like the redemption of our Lord Jesus Christ reaches all of man, our mission will be to “prolong the Incarnation ton all man, in all of man, and in all the manifestations of man”. And because as Redeemer He did as such, we would like to also practice the corporal works of mercy. Those in which, giving a concrete testimony of charity will win many men for the kingdom of Christ, giving glory to God and saving many souls, fulfilling in this manner our universal end. Fulfilling as well with the specific end of our family, “as testimony, firstly, to all the members of our religious institutes that “charity, and only charity will save the world. Blessed are those who have the grace of being victims of charity” and of that charity is indispensable for the evangelization of the culture, as the end worked for, and the end of the work, in any contrary case, one will never reach “the civilization of love”.

The religious of our Institute who dedicates herself specifically to the works of mercy much bring forth to its fullness a fertile spiritual maternity, …this maternity will be able to express itself as a solicitude for men, especially for the most needy: the sick, the handicaps, the abandoned, the orphans, the elderly, the children, the youth, the homebound, etc…

A consecrated woman encounters in this way the Bridegroom, different and unique, in all and each one, according to his same words “when have you done something for one of these and have not done it for me?” (Mt. 25: 40).

Chapter I: The works of Mercy in General

All the works of charity that we will be able to do to benefit others, suppose from our neighbor a necessity and in us the desire to remediate him, under the impulse of the virtue of mercy. Precisely mercy, which is the act of charity, moves us to exercise benevolence, which is its exterior act, more typical and characteristics.

Mercy is one the virtues which refers to the neighbor that is most recommended in Sacred Scripture. “The merciful does well to himself; one with a hard heart, condemns himself” (Pv 11: 17).; “I prefer mercy rather than sacrifice…” (Hos 6:6). Our Lord puts us as model to his Father: “Be merciful as your Heavenly Father is merciful” (Lk 6:36) and moreover makes of it the object of a beatitude: “blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy” (Mt 5:7).

What is mercy? St. Thomas Aquinas, following Saint Augustine, defines it as “a type of internal compassion before the present misery, which moves and impels us to release it if possible”. It is called mercy because it makes man’s heart compassionate before the present misery (“miserum cor”).

Following the merciful compassion of the human misery, it occurs that we are sorrowful of the present evils or miseries for a double motive: “either because we love our neighbor in such a way that his disgraces affect us as if they were our own, or because the present importunacy can easily become ours and submerge us in an identic calamity”. For that reason, the elderly and weak are more inclined to mercy that the strong and powerful, whose abilities does not help them in overcoming evil. This is particularly applicable to a woman, for a “woman has a comprehensible heart, which permits her to confer a delicate and concrete style to charity.

This is how our mercy has this double foundation. In exchange, only God is compassionate of us, because he loves us as his own.

What is the dignity of the virtue of mercy? St. Thomas answers:

“In itself, mercy is the highest of all virtues, for it corresponds to watch over the unfornate, and remediate their deficiencies or disgrace, what properly belongs to the superior. For this reason, mercy is most proper of God and in it shines His omnipotence in the highest level”.

“With relation to who has it, mercy is not the greatest virtue, for it doesn’t make the one who possesses the greatest, that is to say, that he has none above him, but all under him; hence, for the one who holds one above him, it is for him greater and better to unite himself to the superior than to remedy the defect of the inferior. For this reason, for man that has God for superior, charity, with which he unites himself to Him, is better and more excellent than mercy with which he helps the deficiencies of his neighbor. But, among all the virtues that looks to the neighbor, mercy is the highest because its act is also superior, for it does not limit itself to compassion for the present miseries, but also remedies them, and this is what is proper of the superior and the better”.

Benevolence properly is an act of the virtue of charity, but it depends on mercy when this moves us to help the neighbor in his needs, in such a way that the other works of benevolence coincide with the words of mercy, for they are its exterior act, realized under the interior impulse of mercy. Benevolence manifest itself principally in charity in relation to corporal things, and by fraternal correction in what refers to spiritual things; but also, it belongs to it all that is called works of mercy, from which one of the most important is the apostolate, directed to the neighbor practicing the good and with it reaching eternal happiness.

All that is done under the impulses of mercy for the good of the neighbor is a true work of mercy. But the tradition of the Church from the ancient times lists fourteen; seven corporal and seven spiritual. St. Thomas studied the works of mercy when speaking of Charity, which is a part of benevolence, and also divided them into seven corporals and seven spiritual in conformity with the diverse deficiencies of the neighbor.

Chapter II: The corporal works of Mercy

To give food to the hungry

To give drink to the thirsty

The clothe the naked

To give alms to the pilgrim

To visit the sick

To visit the prisoners

To bury the dead

“A particular way to give glory to God is the limitless trust in His Providence, based on His design of salvation, that manifest itself in an eminent way in the Incarnation”.

“The doors of our houses will not ask who is entering, if he has a name, but only if it has a pain, The love of Christ impels us (2 Cor 5: 14)”.

In general, by the highest testimony of charity that it signifies, these works must be a preoccupation of all the members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. In consequence, it will attend with diligence and in a personal manner to the poor and needy, in a special way, to those who are lacking what is indispensable for a life worthy of dignity.

“The poor are Christ: ‘they represent the image of the Song of God’; the pilgrims are Christ: ‘receive them as the same Christ’; the children are Christ, the one who receives them ‘receives me’ (Mt. 18:5); in all men, it is Jesus hidden in the depth of his soul’. Hence said St. Augustine: ‘in Him we are christs and Christ’”.

Article 1: To give food to the hungry

It is one of the most urgent and indispensable works of Mercy, because although those of the spiritual order are more important, by prudence the oportune moment to exercise it can differ, as is the case with fraternal correction; on the contrary, the hungry cannot wait.

It is sure thing that in the world today there is hunger, and that instead of bettering the situation, it becomes worse each time. A problem that is thrown into the hands of hopelessness and of human degradation of the multitude of our brothers in the five continents of the terrestrial globe.

Saddness is another emotional sign of the people that live in a cronic hunger; sadness that not even the stimulating action of alcoholism can extinguish.

The hungry, finally, under his diverse forms, drags along with himself a great load of miseries and moral degradation.

Our religious family considers that global solution of the problem will give in base to the practice of a strict justice, completed by the most beloved charity.

For this reason, it will be precise to establish in the world social justice, as it is understood and propagated by the Catholic Church. Our institute will try to diffuse the social doctrine of the Church through conferences, courses, systematic studies in our communities and especially houses of formation. But it is not only because of lack of knowledge that this doctrine has not been implanted in the world, but more because of egoism, and definitely because of lack of charity. Therefore, this formation on the social doctrine must be integral, instilling intellectually the principles of social justice, but at the same time forming men capable of molding it with charity.

Charity, in effect, is the unique solution, complete and adequate, of the problem of hunger. When we assert to see in our hungering neighbor a brother who is suffering, a suffering member of Christ, the generous and splendid rescue will spontaneously blossom like a sweet exigency of Christian Charity.

“As to the poor, we must always have them be with us, over all giving them food. We will not be afraid that there will not be enough for us, God is never outdone in generosity.

Article 2: To give drink to the thirsty

This new work of mercy is nothing more than a supplement or partial aspect of the latter.

“Meet the thirsty, bring them water; you who dwell in the land of Tema, greet the fugitives with bread.” (Is. 21:14).

“'Come, you who are blessed by my Father… for I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (Mt. 25: 35).

“Anyone who gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ, amen, I say to you, will surely not lose his reward.” (Mk. 9: 41). Not always will one be able to give food to the poor, but a little gesture of charity of a cup of water for love of Christ.

Article 3: To clothe the naked

To set out to relieve these necessities is a great work of charity and mercy. We must not forget that in the condemning sentence of Christ, this inexorable clause is figured: “Because I was naked and you did not clothe me” (Mt 25:43); while in the contrary, the other gives a guarantee of eternal salvation: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (Mt 25: 36).

One of the most opportune ways with which our Institute will be able to exercise this great work of mercy, is to contribute to it with the greatest generosity, to the sustainment of wardrobe of charity where the circumstances require them.

It will be moreover appraisable to ferment among our lay people this works of mercy. Among other things, they can promote traditional pious works, such as dressing a poor child on the day of Christmas, in memory of the Child of Bethlehem, or dressing the whole family on the day of the Holy Family, or dressing children of indigenous families for their First Communion, etc…

Article 4: To give alms to the pilgrim

In ancient times, this work of mercy was one of the most beautiful and frequent, given the abundance of wanderers and pilgrims.

The ancient monastic orders considered Christian hospitality as something sacred and inviolable. In particular, the Rule of St. Benedict.

“Receive all the strangers that come to the monastery as if you were receiving the same Christ, after he will have to say: I was a stranger, and you received me (Mt 25:35). And give to all the honor that is due to them, especially to our brothers in the faith (Gal 6:10) and to the pilgrims. Hence, following the announcement of any stranger, the superior and the monks will set off for the encounter with the most obsequious charity”.

“In the world of today, there is a considerable revolution in this order of things, nevertheless, we can still practice today this work of mercy in our houses giving lodging to visiting religious and families, as long as it does not affect gravely the internal order of the house.

In the world today there is presented a grave problem intimately related to the work of mercy that we are speaking about: the problem of housing. This brings disastrous consequences that this situation has to produce in the physical, intellectual, and moral order of the peoples.

In many places, diverse persons of all sexes, ages, and conditions live piled up together.

Our Institute will form lay people that, having a clear conscience of this problem, are disposed to act, in the first place, succeeding the state test, and that being able to intervene in great scale will give a global solution to the problem.

Lastly, our Institute will be able to intervene directly through the creation of Nursing homes, homes for children, residences for youth, etc...

Article 5: To visit the sick

The key to the problem of suffering, one of whose inexorable manifestations is sickness, is only given through Divine Revelation.

God does not make suffering. Hi primitive plan for humanity excluded it positively. But with the catastophe of original sin, God handed over to man all classes of physical and moral sufferings (Gen 3: 16-19) and removed the preternatural gifts of integrity, impassibility, and immortality. As the consequence the body was left subject to suffering, to sickness, and to death “and thus death came to all, inasmuch as all sinned” (Rom 5: 12).

But sickness more than being a chastisement, is also medicine that not only heals, but also can preserve from future sins and move to good. It can follow that one who has not committed any faults is assailed in temporal things so that he may look for the spiritual which is superior. Many of the afflictions of the present life are hence permitted by God solely to humiliate us and try us.

Sickness as well is an instrument of salvation, for many men have thence encountered God. Also it is a fount of grace for all the good Samaritans that exercise this work of mercy: doctors, nurses, etc. For this reason, it is as well very important the apostolate with doctors, assistants, nurses, etc…

The sick as well as all who lovingly take care of him, obtain many graces, not only for themselves, but also for the whole Church. St. Paul says that he fulfills in his flesh what is lacking in sufferings of Christ through his body which is the Church. Therefore, no one but the sick can better complete with his meritorious suffering the work of the Redemption. “and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if only we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom 8:17).

The religious must know how to teach the sick to suffer and the value of suffering, just as Christ who became one with us to be able to save us, it is permitted us to do the same as well… “Without our suffering, it will not be an excellent social work and service, but neither will it be the work of Christ, and it will not form part of the Redemption” for the “Cross is the only way of life, the sign of the predestined, the scepter of the kingdom of holiness, … ‘ it is the fountain of all blessings, the origin of all graces’”.

This work of mercy must be practiced with a true Christian spirit, which supposes, before all, the intention to thank God, serving him in the members of Christ. It is for him that while this work is a true fountain of merits for the one who does it, it must be realized with faith, seeing in the sick the same Christ who suffers in one of the members of the Mystical Body “Come you blessed of my Father… because I was sick and you visited me” (Mt 25: 34-40). When another spirit does not move us to give completely of ourselves, it is then that the sense of this work of mercy is completed. This is not to say that other human finalities does not move us with the visit: to cure the sick, the console them, to comfort the family, etc., but the formality of all this must be to attend the sick as a suffering member of Christ.

Following charity, the principal motor, we must fundamentally preoccupy ourselves of the spiritual health of the sick, animating him and lifting up in a holy manner his sickness, to see in it the expression of the merciful will of God, and preparing him for the worthy reception of the Holy Sacraments. Sickness makes it possible for many sick people to approach for the first time the sacraments, it is for that that our solicitude will be very important, working with his family and especially when this oppose itself to the Sacraments of Confession and the Anointing of the Sick by fear of the fear that this will produce in the patient. Due to the psychological alteration in which the sick find themselves, it will be more convenient to arm ourselves with patience and abnegation in order to fulfill its exigencies. Same with prudence and delicacy in order to avoid disliking him or afflicting him or rousing in the soul sentiments of rancor, impatience and other similar things, creating a climate of peace which is founded on the knowledge that God does not allow evil but with a gaze at the greater good.

Our Institute will show particular solicitude in the exercise of this work of mercy, trying with all means that they be no sick without spiritual attention nor who come to die without receiving the Holy Sacraments.

In our houses of formation, this idea must be inculcated. The religious will put great care in the attention of the sick, above all in the ones that are in grave situation, so that all the activities of the religious must be oriented to the salvation of the souls and will be a grave responsibility before God if because of her negligence or fault of zeal, one of these souls die without due spiritual attention, which includes, according to CIC; the apostolic blessing with plenary indulgence in the article of the dead which will be procured to the sick.

We must put all the means for the attention of the sick members of the Institute, given that they are “key pieces” of our religious family.

As well the Lay people who in some manner are instilled to our religious Institute will need to be formed in this respect. Especially those who deal directly with the sick as for doctors and nurses; organizing in the measure possible, courses, conferences, congress of training, etc., in order to serve better the sick, helping so that others may participate in his service.

It is important to have present the obligations that a catholic doctor has. He must in his part take account of this, yet at the cost of sacrifices and extraordinary studies, to bring back the health of the sick; to freely attend to the poor sick; to never attempt to go against the health, nor the life of the soul in order to save the body, even it be the difficult parts, trying to save the life of the mother and the child never without attempting to go directly against the life of one of the two, nor never provoking abortion to save the mother, baptizing any aborted fetus in the form prescribed by the Church, even if it is few days, never giving immoral advises in the pretext of corporal health and advising with time the family and the priest for the administration of the Sacraments.

It is of capital importance in our days, now being for the high testimony of charity that are offered, as for the gravity and the risk that are enclosed for society many sickness or situations such as AIDS, homosexuality, drug addiction, etc. that our Institute studies this problem in order to later try to solve it in a concrete manner.

One will be able to occupy herself of all the aforementioned by way of chaplaincies, lay groups, and included the erection of centers of first help, dispensaries, hospitals or houses of special internship, were the situation obliges it.

Another way to visit the sick will be to bring the pilgrim image of any devotion of our Lady, now that “Mary Most Holy continues being the loving Consolation of much physical and moral pains, that afflict and torment humanity. She knows our suffering and our pains because she as well suffered, since Bethlehem to Calvary: ‘ and a sword will pierce your heart’”, and as well incorporating the sick in any confraternity in which he can offer his suffering for the salvation of souls, etc.

Article 6: To Redeem the captive

The spirit who informed this great work of mercy in the centuries in which it had immediate application (some Religious Orders were founded, principally that of the Trinitarians, founded by St. John of Mata and approved by Inocent III in 1198, and the Mercedarians, founded by Saint Peter Nolasco and Saint Raymond of penafort and approved by Gregory IX in 1235) can be expanded today in various forms, principally visiting prisoners to bring them our help and our advise and redeeming the moral and material slavery of so many disgraceful victims of the same.

a). Visit to the prisoners

Our Lord reminds us of that phrase which will sound with the judgement: “I was in prison and you did not visit me” (Mt 25:43). Saint Paul says: “Remember the prisoners, as if you yourself were a prisoner with them, and of those who suffer bad treatement, as if it was in your body” (Heb 13:3).

Our Institute will have to put particular interest in the apostolate of Jail, following the weel of the Incarnate Word who came to free the captives and oppressed, for all that was anteriorly mentioned and because the correct meaning of prisons has been lost in our days, now that they are converted in spiritual prisons. In this way, great importance will be given to the periodical visit and catechesis to the prisoners. We have the example of St. Joseph Cafasso, who awoke religious vocations from the women’ jails, as the life written by the Cardinal Carlos Salotti relates to us. In this way, one will look to provide them with good literature and if possible, to help his family spiritually as well as materially.

b). The redemption of moral and material slavery

Moreover, other forms of slavery can be: work; men trapped into economical ambitions; drugs; alcoholism, etc.

These diverse forms of moral and material captivity can be suppressed or alleviated by Christian charity, for that reason, our Institute in the midst of its possibilities will look to alleviate these situations, showing the true meaning of life and the place things must have, teaching men how to have fun, to rejoice in the true Christian joy.

Article 7: to bury the dead

The cadaver of a Christian is a sacred relic. During his life he was the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 6:19), and one day, at the command of the word of God, it will gloriously resurrect from among the dead, to be eternally happy in mansions glory (1 Ts 4: 13 – 18).

Nevertheless, the cadaver of a man inspires of itself horror, and consequently is a work of mercy toward the deceased, to remove him from the sight of men and to give him a christian burial.

It is here the recompense that one obtains from God for her charity, communicated by the archangel Raphael to the same Tobias: “when you, Tobit, and Sarah prayed, it was I who presented and read the record of your prayer before the Glory of the Lord; and I did the same thing when you used to bury the dead. When you did not hesitate to get up and leave your dinner in order to go and bury the dead, I was sent to put you to the test. At the same time, however, God commissioned me to heal you and your daughter-in-law Sarah. I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who enter and serve before the Glory of the Lord." (Tb 12: 12-15).

The death of a dear being signifies a great pain. It is for this reason that showing affection, charity and compassion, united to the cadaver of a dear being reaches to the depths of the soul, and his memory will never leave a thankful heart.

As well, it is a great work of mercy given that if comforts the private debtors of a dear being and makes his heart turn more probably towards God, for the testimony of charity which it signifies, and because strengthened in the faith and in hope grants him to value the ephemeral of this life, and the permanent of eternal life.

Our Institute will consider of vital importance this type of apostolate which in another way is a field each time more invaded by the sects, with the fatal consequences which follow from them.

resuming what must be our spirit in the practice of the works of mercy, let us remember the exhortation of Mother Teresa: “we are not here for the work. we are for Jesus. Before all we are religious. not social assistants, teachers, nurses, doctors. we serve Jesus in the poor…all that we do… all for Him. Our life do not have another meaning. This is the thing that many do not understand. We serve Jesus 24 hours a day and He gives us strength. We love Him in the poor and the poor with Him, but always the Lord first”. 1

Chapter 3: SPIRITUAL WORKS OF MERCY

To teach the ignorant

To give counsel to the needy

To correct the wrong

To console the sad

To forgive injuries

To suffer with patience the one who afflict us

To pray to God for the living and the dead

These works are the ones who are more oriented towards our cultural end, for we are conscious that the great battle of our time is intellectual, given that it consists in eliminating error, fundamentally the sin against light, of militant atheism, of liberalism to the maximum, of the ideologies, of all idolatries, and in the last place of the ignorance of God.

Article 1: To teach the ignorant

We have here one of the greatest works of mercy that we can exercise for the benefit of the neighbor. The human intelligence has a thirst for truth over all for the transcendental and eternal Truth revealed by the Incarnate Word, and they are so many that have not encountered it yet, or at least have not glimpsed at it completely.

So it is understood that the principal ignorance of this work of mercy must take care of dissipating, is the one which refers to religion and the eternal destiny of man. There is no worse ignorance than what this refers to, although a great saying or nobel prize suffers it in the order of human knowledge.

Saint Paul warns us explicitly that “the wisdom of this world is nothingness before God” (1 Cor 3:19). Nevertheless, however in small steps, it is also a great work of mercy to teach the ignorant the things that they need for their human life here in the world, for grace builds on nature.

Certainly, it will be important to offer to the individual through education the means necessary for employ themselves in society. And like this our colleges will be able to be oriented to teach and read and write to the poor and illiterate, faciliting the indispensable mean as for an intellectual education proportional to his talent. This will be repeated in the high schools, and universities. But the fundamental end that we must move toward in the educational apostolalte, will be to form youths that have a “spirit of principle”, youth that distinguish but do not separate the human and the divine as is demonstrated in the Incarnate Word. Youths that want a world where lay people and religious united, fight so that truth and virtue might reign. Hence, it seems to us that all our educational establishments, primary, secondaries, and superior must bring forth in its midst the impression of a true human and theological formation. Feeding itself in the classical culture and in the permanent values of the spirit and of faith, for it is faith the one that allows man to attain the highest object of the intellect, which is God. And in this manner to edify over the rock which is Christ, the only mean to inculturate the Gospel. Only in this way will we be able to bring souls “to the unity of the faith and the full knowledge of the Son of God, to the state of the perfect man, attaining the stature proper to the whole Christ” (Eph. 4: 13).

Another way to teach the one who does not know is to publish, propagate, and profusely distribute books, pamphlets, journals, newpapers, religious articles, computer programs, etc. “Through the oral and written word, we want to prolong the Word”. For it, we must count with our own editorials.

Also, this must realize itself through the apostolate of modern means of communication, through all types of recording, whether videos or audios, as well as radios and television programs. For all, this is precisely to dispose of all the equipment necessary.

To collaborate with all the means at our reach for the great work of the propagation of the faith among the unfaithful world. There are more than 2,000 millions of pagans in the entire world that have not yet received that message of Jesus Christ, nor consequently baptism. For that reason, it seems to us indispensable that our Institute, prioritize that foundations in mission lands. For this, we must form suitable missionaries in the ministry of the word, catechisis, popular missions, spiritual retreats, etc. And so well the best mean to help the missions consists, without any doubt, to offer them missionaries, and this as well will be able to bring us to implement an adequate pastoral to attract native vocations.

Article 2: To give good counsel to the one who needs it

Many are the souls who give the definitive orientation of their lives to the way of the good to a good advice given opportunely by a friend or a good person who separated them from an irreparable going astray. There are personal situations that cannot revolve itself with agreement for the own interest, but which need the orientation and advice of a prudent and experiemented person.

But it is necessary that the advice feeds on charity, in such a way that one advised can really make use it. For this reason, one must evade from showing airs of superiority to the advised, and of the advice and occasion of shame and humiliation in front of the others.

This work of mercy speaks of a special reference to paternity, because it is proper to fathers to advise. Hence our religious must be true spiritual mothers, which implies a coherence of life and faith, in order to give effective advices over all in spiritual matters.

Also, great importance will be given to form lay people in this way. It is rightful that the fathers illumine their children with their advices.

Article 3: To correct the wrong

Fraternal correction is one of the greatest works of mercy. By fraternal correction, it is understood “the warning done to the culpable neighbor in private and for pure charity to separate him from sin”. It will be done in private and for pure charity because it is not justice that obliges it, but love; it will procure the reprehension of evil in so far as evil will wound the one who execute it, and not insofar as it wounds the common good or the good of a third party.

It is evident that if we have the natural obligation to help the neighbor in his corporal necessities, with greater motives will we have the obligation to help him in his spiritual necessities. “if your brother sins against you, go and reproach him in secret. If he listens to you, you will have won your brother over.” (Mt 18: 15). “If you are careless to correct, you will be worse than the one who sinned”.

We must practice this work of Mercy primarily in our religious family but also with anyone who needs it and always imbued with charity, patience, humility, prudence and discretion. The practice of fraternal correction, as it is described and pointed out in the Constitutions, will need to be a true distinction of our love for our neighbor.

In this respect as well, it will receive particular importance in our time, given the great confusion of ideas and the facility of its expansion, to direct this work of mercy towards the refutation of errors, knowing that we must hate the sin and not the sinner. And this for two reasons: first, for the good of the one erring, so that he may come out of his error. Second, for the common good, to correct the damages that the diffusion of the error has produced.

Article 4: To console the sorrowful

Sadness is a passion that comes from the appetite, in face of a present evil. Among all the passions, it is the one who harms more the body; St. Thomas Aquinas says: “it puts itself against the life of man with regard to the essence of its movement, and not only in respect to his medium or quantity as the other passions of the soul."2

Each day there is more sadness in the world because each time there is more misery and less love to alleviate it. Many souls which have lost the illusion to live lie in graves in a great sadness and moral atmosphere, produced by the terrible fight with existence, the unsatisfied vital necessities, the reverse of fortune, imcomprehensions, sickenesses and death of dear ones. In these conditions, few charitable works can bring back the peace and joy life to many of these souls. But there can be nor can there be a more radical and profound consolation than the one who springs from the truths of the faith, for it shows that no disgrace is total and definitive, except the eternal lost of God. This is the fundamental idea that must come out of the souls beaten down by sadness.

St. Thomas Aquinas, among the five remedies that can be opposed to sadness, numerates delight, the contemplation of truth, and the compassion of friends.

Delight is certaintly the repose of the appetite in a connatural good, in turn sadness comes from what is contrary to the appetite. And so, like all rest of the body is a remedy against any fatigue which provokes it in any natural cause, equally delight is a remedy to mitigate all sadness, whichever is within its providence.

Following this idea, our religious family will be able to alleviate many souls depressed by real or apparent evils, giving testimony of the Christian joy. This will be done individually by each of its members, or by means of artistic representations, musicals, theatres of any other type, which delight in the licit good of the said souls.

With this end, the testimony of the Christian joy acquires much relief, which our communities must give, in such a way that it can be said of them what was said of the first Christian: “ See how they love each other”. Our communities must show how the love of Christ separates from the darkness of sadness.

Analogically, in the interior of the community, a culminating moment in the practice of this work is constituted by the Eutrapelial activities in which trough the generous giving of each one to the communitarian recreation, joy is consequently brought forth.

The greatest delight that we can reach in this life is the contemplation of the truth, and given that all delight diminishes pain and sadness, we must conclude that delight in the truth is one of the most efficatious remedies against sadness.

All that is done to contemplate thetranscendental truth of God will be a great remedy therefore against sadness. This will necessarily bring one to contemplate the beauty of the Supreme Being. Beauty which participated to man, is encountered reflected principally in the great artistic works of humanity. Trough this, all that we do to diffuse and know the great works of art, painting, sculpture, music, etc. will be a highly positive contribution to the expansion of the human spirit which will alleviate it from the weight of sadness from small evils.

A friend who sympathizes with the sorrows of the other is naturally a consoler. First because he alleviates and lightens the burden of the neighbor, imitating our Lord who offers us His alleviation and rest. Second, because the condolence of a friend is a sign of love, and to feel loved is always consolation and joy.

Article 5: To pardon injuries

This work of mercy constitute at the same time, an indispensable work of charity for the person itself, given aht the pardon of the neighbor depends that God pardons us, remembering always that “Charity covers a multitude of sins”.

The doctrine of Christ is clear and does not require any commentary: “You have heard it been said: you shall love your neighbor and hate your enemies. but I say to you: love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you so that you may be children of your father, who is in heaven, and who makes the sun rise over the bad and good and pours rain over the just and the unjust” (Mt 5: 43-45). Christ clearly explained this doctrine in the servant who owned ten thousand talents.

From this, we can deduce that this is not only a simple advise of perfection that we can accept or refuse without compromising our future salvation, all who want to persevere in the grace of God must forgive from all their heart, accepting this divine law.

Moreover, we must imitate Christ who practiced this doctrine in a heroic and sublime way especially on the cross. “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Lk 23: 34), and later he forgives the repentant thief: “I tell you solemnly, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Lk 23: 43).

Also, we must follow the example of the saints, among many, the example of St. Jane de Chantal, who became the godmother in baptism of one of the children of the assassin of her husband.

For this forgiveness to be authentically Christian, it must be Prompt “do not let the sun set on your anger” (Eph 4:26). Spontaneous, as is indicated in (Mt 5:23) that before presenting the offering, we must first forgive our brother. Unlimited, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times” (Mt 18:22). From the heart, not only the external forgiveness “Then in anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he should pay back the whole debt. So will my heavenly Father do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from his heart.” (Mt 18: 34-35). And for love of God, this is the most important condition for our forgiveness to be Christian and meritorious.

Our family of the Institute of the Incarnate Word will need to put special attention in the fulfillment of this work of mercy, loving our enemies and praying for those who persecute us, also included is a fact experienced for us that our greatest enemies have converted to be our greatest benefactors.

On account of the communitarian dimension, it is important to point out here in the paper the chapter of faults, in which the mercy not only must bring forgiveness to injuries, but also leads to profess greater esteem to the one who accuses himself.

Article 6: To suffer with patience those who trouble us

Saint Paul in prison wrote to the Christians in Ephesus: “I, then (…) to live in a manner worthy of the call you have received, (…) bearing with one another through love, striving to preserve the unity of the spirit through the bond of peace”3. In fact, charity must bring us to surpass the differences of temperaments, opinions, and ways of being that manifest itself in community life. Since it is only by means mutual comprehension and tolerance that it is possible to conserve peace and hope among men. “What man cannot correct in himself or in others must be supported with patience until God orders it in another way.”4

The ultimate sustenance of all imperfections is the hereditary pain of original sin, who in other parts offers us the possibility of suffering for God on behalf of our brothers, as they suffer on our behalf.

Let us not forget that it belongs to small souls to see small defects in great men.5 Hence we must not allow little imperfections of our brothers to impede us from seeing the wonders that the grace of God realizes in them.

We also know that the Providence of God in respect material things is much less than its relation with spiritual things. For this reason, the damages in material things must not retract us from fomenting the spiritual goods.

This work of mercy must be exercise with all men, but we have the opportunity to practice it more correctly with our brothers in religion, in whom generally there is no intention to harm us, but even if there were, we will still be obliged to fulfill this work of mercy. “I have become all things to all, to bring them to Jesus Christ” 6

Article 7: To pray to God for the living and the dead

Charity is a friendship that has as its fundamental the common participation in the eternal Beatitude. Therefore we are obliged to practice this charity helping within our capacities, that all those who are able capable of salvation may arrive at it. The only ones that are excluded are demons of hell and the condemned.

It is clear and evident that with relation to the immense majority of men who live on earth, and the souls in purgatory, we cannot exercise our charity more than through prayer. To pray for the living and the dead is as well an indeclinable exigency of Christian charity.

In general, we must ask for all those to who we can extend our charity but in a special way we must ask for the most needy: the poor, pagans, sinners, dead, sick, etc. For those closest to us: brothers in religion, parents, friends, etc. For benefactors. For those who hear us or have hurt us.

Our Institute will need to inculcate in each one of its members the obligation to exercise this work of mercy. And moreover will offer sufferings and prayers, especially the Holy Mass, for its deceased members, the intention of the superiors, benefactors, enemies, etc.
